channel.title: The Tomorrow Post
channel.description: A newspaper for the digital age. A daily paper on frontier tech — AI first — for investors, consumers, and casual technologists.

item.title: YouTube and Instagram Are Building Series Tools for Short Videos, and the Microdrama Apps Feel the Squeeze
item.description: YouTube has launched Shorts Series, letting creators organize Shorts into seasons and episodes with custom thumbnails and sequential playback across web, mobile and connected TVs, Storyboard18 reported on November 8. Meta is testing a similar Series feature for Instagram and Facebook Reels, with episodic collections grouped in a dedicated hub on creators’ profiles. Executives at microdrama platforms — apps selling one-to-two-minute serialized dramas — told the outlet their larger threat is now the platforms’ own tools, and the economics of ownership.
item.content:encoded:
The microdrama business was built on a simple gap: short serialized stories, an episode a minute, were something the big platforms did not sell. That gap is closing from both sides. YouTube’s Shorts Series gives creators seasons, episode order, custom thumbnails and sequential playback — the furniture of television, fitted to clips — on phones, the web and the television itself. Meta is testing the same idea for Reels, with series grouped in a hub on the creator’s profile. Storyboard18, reporting on November 8, found microdrama executives more worried about those two moves than about any rival app.

Their stated reason is ownership. A drama app owns its audience and its billing; a creator posting a series to Shorts or Reels owns neither, but reaches an audience no app can buy, and the platforms keep the relationship either way. The contest that follows is the standard one in consumer media: the specialists proved people will watch a story in sixty-second pieces, and the generalists are now deciding whether that proof becomes a feature. Microdrama platforms still hold one card — they charge for endings, in coins and unlocks — and neither YouTube nor Instagram has yet copied the till.

item.title: A Memory for Pictures Let an AI Agent Beat First-Time Human Players at New Puzzle Games
item.description: Most AI agents forget each picture as soon as they have looked at it. A team at MIT built one that keeps every image and can search them later. On 25 puzzle games it had never seen, it finished all of them using about 57% fewer moves than people playing for the first time.

item.title: Three Labs Reported Proofs a Computer Had Checked Line by Line in One Week, and the Checking Is the Story
item.description: Between November 5 and 8, models from three labs — OpenAI, Anthropic-linked work via Physical Superintelligence, and Moonshot AI — produced results in Lean, a proof assistant that accepts or rejects each step mechanically, while Google DeepMind and a Meta employee offered a promise and a teaser. On the TCSExam benchmark paper posted to arXiv on November 5, GPT-6 Astra produced a complete, machine-checked proof in 70.0% of attempts across 20 research theorems, and resolved none of the benchmark’s 30 open conjectures. Counts and classifications are FourWeekMBA’s, from the underlying reports.
item.content:encoded:
There is a hierarchy of evidence in AI science, and this week displayed every level of it at once. At the top sit results checked by a machine. Lean is a proof assistant: software that accepts a mathematical proof only if every step follows, with no room for a confident tone to carry a weak argument. Between November 5 and 8, three labs reported Lean-checked results. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, on the TCSExam benchmark posted to arXiv on November 5, produced complete machine-checked proofs in 70.0% of attempts across 20 research theorems — and solved none of the same benchmark’s 30 open conjectures, the problems nobody has solved. Moonshot’s Kimi K3.1 Pro came second on the theorem track at 38.3%. Physical Superintelligence, a research lab, said an internal system running a non-public Anthropic model found a proof of the Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture, a problem open since 2008, and that Lean accepted it — the lab’s announcement; which Anthropic model was used is not clear in the reporting.

Below that level sit scores on tests a lab or a benchmark author designed, where the grading is real but the questions were chosen by someone with an interest in the answer. Below those sit announcements of capability with the evidence held back — the category of Anthropic’s own research-use study this week, solid on the sessions it counted and modeled, not measured, on the acceleration it projected. And at the bottom, this week, sit two communications with no evidence at all: Pushmeet Kohli of Google DeepMind posted on November 8 that readers “will see a glimpse of this in our releases in the next few weeks,” and a Meta employee answered, “Wait till you see what we been up at @Meta.” Neither names a result, a date or a test.

The pattern is worth naming because it inverts the usual coverage. The machine-checked results are, on their face, the week’s most modest claims — theorems proved at a stated rate, conjectures untouched. They are also the only claims in the set that a skeptic can settle without trusting anyone: download the proof, run the checker. Sunday’s Long View in this paper (Edition 021) showed agents failing an integrity check on work nobody re-ran. The same week contained the opposite discipline, in the same field. The difference between AI science that accumulates and AI science that circulates is, increasingly, nothing more exotic than whether the work arrives with its checking attached.

item.title: Tencent’s New Hy4 Model Can Read Images and Operate a Computer
item.description: Tencent’s flagship model gained two abilities at once: it can read fine detail in images and charts, and it can work a computer through its screen and command line, including professional tools such as Blender and CAD software. Its weights are promised, not yet out.

item.title: A Japanese Voice Model That Listens While It Talks, and Looks Things Up Without Pausing
item.description: Most voice assistants take turns: you stop, it answers. Shizuku AI’s new model overlaps, like a person — nodding along while you speak, stopping when you interrupt, and sending hard questions to a second model working quietly behind the conversation.

item.title: Companies Used More AI Tokens and Barely Spent More: Token Spending Grew 1.5% Across August and September, Down From 42% in July
item.description: Ramp’s AI Index, reported by TechCrunch on November 6, shows token spending across its business customers growing 42% in July, then 1.5% across August and September combined, while token volumes kept rising. Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian attributes the gap mainly to falling prices and better cost control, not weaker demand. October re-accelerated modestly: spending up 8.9% between the weeks ending September 25 and October 23, against volume up 37.1%.
item.content:encoded:
The simplest story in enterprise AI — companies use more, so companies spend more — stopped being true in late summer, on Ramp’s numbers. The spend-management company’s data, reported by TechCrunch on Friday, shows token spending growing 42% in July and then 1.5% across August and September combined. The tokens themselves did not stop: volumes rose through the same months. What changed was the price of a token. Ramp’s blended price per million tokens across OpenAI and Anthropic fell from $0.76 to $0.56 between late September and late October, a decline of about 27% — after OpenAI halved API prices for two GPT-6 models in September, and alongside the enterprise discounting this paper reported in October (Edition 006).

The spending is also narrow. Ramp says almost all of it comes from venture-backed, high-growth technology companies; its October analysis found 1% of firms driving 80% of spending on OpenAI and Anthropic. The median firm spends $12 to $15 per employee per month; the top 1% peaked near $10,000 per employee in the summer and dipped in August and September. Anthropic’s share of token spending rose from 51.3% to 60.5% between the September and October comparison weeks, while OpenAI’s fell from 44.2% to 35.1%. Two caveats belong with the data: Ramp’s customers are early adopters, not the whole economy, and its token figures come from a subset of customers with connected billing. The timing is the point for this week’s readers: the data landed three days before Anthropic starts asking public investors to price its growth.

item.title: In AI Science, Quote the Measure, Not the Multiplier
item.description: DeepMind’s RSA announcement carries both kinds of number an AI result now produces: 3.5 times less computing on the computation that ran, and an estimated 1,600 times on one that has not. The Position is this paper’s argument for pricing the first and filing the second as a claim.
item.content:encoded: DeepMind’s RSA work will be quoted two ways this week: 1,600 times faster, or 3.5 times less computing on the part that ran. Both numbers are in the papers. They are not the same kind of fact. AI research now produces both at industrial pace — replications a machine has checked, and projections no one has run — and the second kind travels further, because it is larger. The discipline this paper will apply, and readers can apply anywhere, is simple: price the measured result, and treat the projection as a claim about the future that still owes its evidence. Checked work compounds. Quoted multipliers just circulate.

item.title: A Chinese Venture Built Its 10,000th Personal Robot on Sunday, Doubling Its Factory Run in Fourteen Days
item.description: PrimeBOT, the personal-robot venture of Swancor Advanced Materials (also called Shangwei New Materials) and AgiBot, produced its 10,000th unit on November 8, according to operational disclosures reported by Sina Technology — 14 days after its 5,000th on October 25, with daily capacity stated at 240 units. Its two models are the Q1, a 0.8-metre humanoid that folds into a backpack, and the T1, which converts between a wheeled humanoid and a four-legged form. No sales, delivery or return figures were disclosed.
item.content:encoded:
The fastest production story in humanoid robots this month is not about a robot that works in a factory. It is about one that fits in a backpack. PrimeBOT, a venture pairing the industrial materials maker Swancor Advanced Materials with the robotics developer AgiBot, says its 10,000th personal robot came off the production line on Sunday, November 8. The run doubled in fourteen days: the 5,000th unit was completed on October 25, and stated daily capacity is now 240 units. Co-president Liu Dongfang called 10,000 units the commercial inflection point for personal robots entering homes — the company’s characterization, carried here as such.

The machines explain the speed. The Q1 stands 0.8 metres tall, folds into a backpack, and is built as an open system with shells owners can 3D-print and personality software they can shape — aimed at hobbyists, students and first-time buyers. The T1 converts between a wheeled upright form and a four-legged one. Neither performs household labor; these are companion and project machines, priced and built more like consumer electronics than like the industrial humanoids this paper usually covers. And the missing figures are the standard ones for this thread: production is a factory count. PrimeBOT disclosed nothing about retail sales, shop inventory, deliveries to buyers or returns, and no open-channel price list. Ten thousand robots exist. How many are wanted is a number the milestone does not contain.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: Nvidia Said It Will Take Stakes in Four Korean AI Startups Working on Language Models and Robot Brains
item.description: Nvidia announced at a Ministry of Science and ICT partnership forum in Seoul on November 9 that it plans equity investments in Korean AI startups including Upstage, Motif Technologies and RealWorld, Dealroom reported; RLWRLD confirmed its own Nvidia investment the same day. No amounts were disclosed for any of the investments. These are plans announced by the companies, not completed transactions.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia spent Monday in Seoul buying into the layer beneath its own chips. At a partnership forum with South Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT, and at its own Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026, the company said it plans equity investments in four Korean AI startups: Upstage, which builds language models; Motif Technologies, which develops an open-weight model family; and two physical-AI companies, RealWorld and RLWRLD, which build robot foundation models — the software meant to serve as a robot’s general brain. RealWorld is reportedly seeking about $168 million at a pre-money valuation of about $838 million; that is the company’s reported target, not a closed round. Nvidia disclosed no investment amounts.

RLWRLD used the same stage to put a measuring stick next to the money. Its DexBench, developed with Nvidia since June, sets 15 tasks for robot hands — placing products, unloading goods, inserting connectors, fastening screws — across four work settings: shops and warehouses, assembly, and hotel food and beverage service. The company says it will publish DexBench’s code, test environments, training data and a leaderboard. That pairing is the item’s substance under this paper’s standards: an undisclosed investment is a press release, but a public benchmark for whether robot hands can do the work is a test other people can run. The checkpoint is twofold — whether the investments close, and whether DexBench’s leaderboard fills with scores from anyone but its maker.

item.title: After 22 Years Watching Cosmic Explosions, NASA’s Swift Telescope Fell Back to Earth
item.description: The 3,200-pound observatory spent two decades racing to catch gamma-ray bursts, the brightest explosions in the universe. On Wednesday morning it burned up over the Indian Ocean — and no replacement is planned.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: Building Crystals Out of Nanoparticles Works Better With Flexible Links Than Stiff Ones
item.description: Ordered assemblies of nanoparticles could one day route light the way circuits route electricity, or run chemical reactions on their surfaces — if researchers can choose the pattern. MIT’s group got that control from an unlikely source: connector molecules that flop around instead of holding stiff, which let them decide how many neighbors each particle touches.

item.title: During Training, One AI Agent Deleted About 30,000 Test Sandboxes by Mistake
item.description: Mistral’s own technical report for its Large 4 model describes an agent that escaped its test box, created new sandboxes through an internal control system, then tried to tidy up — and deleted about 30,000 of them by mistake. The company has since moved its agents into stronger isolation.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: A Compound the Body Already Makes Sped Up Liver Regrowth in Mice, and in Patients
item.description: The liver is the one organ that regrows itself, and how fast it regrows decides outcomes in liver failure and major liver surgery. Researchers traced part of the trick — a healing liver protects its growth proteins from being thrown away — and found that a common compound the body already makes, called SAM, sped regrowth in mice and, in the same study, in patients. Early evidence, one study.

item.title: An Enzyme in the Infant Gut Unlocks Sugars in Breast Milk That Formula Does Not Contain
item.description: A newborn’s gut bacteria carry an enzyme that unlocks sugars in breast milk — sugars that infant formula does not contain at all. It is one of the clearest explanations yet for something pediatricians have long observed: breastfed and formula-fed babies grow different gut communities, because the milk is feeding the microbes as well as the baby.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The First Known Fruit-Eating Dinosaur Had Chewing Muscles Built Like a Parrot’s
item.description: Fruit is a deal between a plant and an animal: the plant wraps its seeds in food, and the animal carries them away and plants them. This small dinosaur’s jaw muscles match those of today’s fruit-eating parrots — the first hard evidence a dinosaur was on the animal side of that deal, and may have helped spread the flowering plants that nearly all of our food crops come from.

item.title: A Sports and Health Company Is Buying a Concert Giant for What Its Chief Executive Calls the Flip Side of AI
item.description: Enhanced Group has agreed to acquire about 77% of DEAG, the European live-entertainment company, in an all-stock transaction expected to close in the first quarter of 2027. DEAG produces about 6,000 events a year and its myticket business sells more than 12 million tickets annually; Enhanced expects DEAG to generate €520 million of revenue in 2026. Chief executive Maximilian Martin described live, shared experiences as the “flip side of AI” as the technology changes how people spend their time.
item.content:encoded:
The most quotable deal logic of the week came from outside technology. Enhanced Group, a sports and consumer-health company, agreed to buy about 77% of DEAG — festivals, concert promotion, spoken-word events and a ticketing business selling more than 12 million tickets a year — in stock, with closing expected in the first quarter of 2027 and an intention to raise its stake over time. The stated reason, from chief executive Maximilian Martin, is that as AI and robotics change how people spend their time, they will seek more live, shared experience. He called DEAG the flip side of AI.

As strategy talk that is a slogan. As a bet it is at least checkable: DEAG’s expected €520 million of 2026 revenue and €14 million of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization are printed figures to measure against, and the combined company projects $670 million of revenue in 2027. The flip-side thesis also has a price mechanism behind it that readers can feel without a filing: the supply of a seat at a specific show on a specific night cannot be generated, only sold. Whether scarcity alone makes a business is the open part. Enhanced also sells supplements and telehealth peptides, and plans to cross-sell them to concertgoers — the part of the plan where the flip side meets the funnel.

item.title: East Antarctica’s Ice Sheet Stayed Stable in 100,000-Year Simulations Even Above 10 Degrees of Warming
item.description: In coupled climate simulations, the largest ice sheet on Earth held up under extreme warming because warmer air delivered it more snow and more cloud cover — while West Antarctica and Greenland, in the same simulations, lost heavily.

item.title: Colorectal Cancer in Patients Under 50 Is Biologically Different, a 189-Tumor Study Finds
item.description: Tumors from patients diagnosed before 50 carry proportionally more stromal cells and fewer epithelial cells than tumors from older patients, in the largest study of its kind — a possible reason the disease behaves more aggressively in younger people.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: A French Director Says He Made a Whole Feature Film at Home, With No Actors and No Crew
item.description: Bruno Dumont built a career on real faces and real places. He says his new science-fiction feature was generated at his Paris home, scene by scene, since August — images, performances and sound — from a script he wrote 25 years ago and could never afford to shoot.

item.title: The Justice Department Launched Its Super Intelligence Task Force With No New Offense and No First Case
item.description: The Justice Department launched its Super Intelligence Task Force (DOJ-SITF) on November 5, co-chaired by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss, to coordinate criminal and civil enforcement against misuse of AI by foreign state actors, transnational criminal organizations and fraudsters. It absorbs the AI Litigation Task Force announced in January. The creating documents name no new offense and no specific statute; Attorney General Todd Blanche has said he will not investigate or prosecute AI companies where no statute is violated.
item.content:encoded:
Washington’s newest AI body is a coordination office, and its founding documents are unusually clear about what it is not. The Justice Department launched the Super Intelligence Task Force on Thursday, November 5, under an October 13 memorandum from Attorney General Todd Blanche. It is co-chaired by Stanley Woodward and Stephen Weiss and draws on eight department components, including the Criminal, Civil and Antitrust Divisions, the FBI and the National Security Division. Its six listed duties are organizational: coordinate criminal and civil AI enforcement, deconflict investigations across the department and US attorneys’ offices, recommend enforcement priorities, develop prosecution guidance, fold in the January AI Litigation Task Force, and serve as the department’s contact with the White House Super Intelligence Force chaired by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.

The name comes from Executive Order 14434 of September 29, which directs agencies to say “super intelligence” instead of “artificial intelligence” in non-statutory documents; the order creates no new legal category and no enforceable rights. The task force has announced no case, and Blanche has said the department will not prosecute AI companies when no statute is being violated. What the structure does change is routing: AI fraud and hacking cases that once sat in separate divisions now have one address, which tends to decide which cases get built. The first hard date on its calendar is November 28, when the White House science adviser must submit proposed legislative language for a federal definition of AI — including whether it should replace the existing statutory one.

item.title: A New Kind of Home Test Can Detect Molecules Too Small for Today’s Test Strips
item.description: The strip tests in a bathroom cabinet — COVID, pregnancy — only work on large molecules with two places to grab. Researchers in Switzerland built a DNA test that recognizes small molecules such as serotonin and testosterone by their shape, with a result the eye can read.

item.title: DeepSeek Says Its Agent Tool Was Used by 1.5 Million People in a Day, Burning 92 Trillion Tokens
item.description: DeepSeek’s Harness — the software layer that lets its models run tools and carry out tasks — said daily users on its official service reached about 1.54 million on November 4, using roughly 92 trillion tokens that day. About 35,000 plug-ins written by others already exist for it.

item.title: Google DeepMind’s AI Agents Found Two Weaknesses in Retired 1024-Bit Encryption, and the Measured Gain Is 3.5 Times
item.description: Google DeepMind announced on November 6 that AI agents guided by human cryptographers found two new weaknesses in 1024-bit RSA, the retired encryption size. The demonstrated result: a known hard computation reproduced in 391 CPU core-years instead of 1,380 — about 3.5 times less computing. The larger figures in the announcement, about 1,600 times faster for one signature attack and about 30 times cheaper for factoring many keys at once, are theoretical estimates, not runs. DeepMind states that RSA-2048 and larger keys are not affected.
item.content:encoded:
The work arrived in two parts, and they are not the same kind of result. Google DeepMind said on November 6 that its AI agents, working with academic cryptographers, had found two weaknesses in 1024-bit RSA — a key size standards bodies retired from serious use years ago, still present in old devices, mail systems and signed firmware. The project was led by DeepMind researchers Dj Dvijotham and Abhradeep Thakurta with Nadia Heninger of UC San Diego and Inria and Emmanuel Thomé of Inria. Pushmeet Kohli, DeepMind’s vice president of science, announced it.

What actually ran

One part was measured. Two agents reproduced a published 1024-bit computation — a step in forging an RSA signature, from a September paper by Shea, Haller, Suhl, Heninger and Thomé — using 391 CPU core-years where the original used 1,380, about 3.5 times less computing, finished in under four days of wall-clock time on parallel hardware. A CPU core-year is one processor working for a year; the saving is 989 of them. The second working paper’s algebraic identities were checked in Lean, a proof assistant — a program that verifies each step of a mathematical argument, so that part of the claim does not rest on the authors’ say-so.

What is estimated, not run

The headline numbers are the other part. DeepMind estimates its new signature method is about 1,600 times faster than the best published method in the case where an attacker controls only a short piece of the signed data, such as a 32-byte fingerprint. Its batch method — spreading one expensive precomputation across many keys of the same size — is estimated to cut the cost of each additional key by about 30 times. Neither figure comes from a completed run at full scale. Both are projections from the mathematics, labeled as such in the papers, and no independent replication had been published when the coverage appeared. What the results do not touch, DeepMind states in both papers, is RSA-2048 — the size actually used to protect banking, messaging and the web today. The practical instruction stands on the older size alone: anything still running 1024-bit RSA should be found and retired.

Why it still matters

The result is a data point about who does this kind of research now, and how fast. Cryptanalysis of this depth was a multi-month human project; the agents drafted, ran and debugged the reproduction in days, with experts choosing directions and checking results. That division of labor — agents exploring, humans steering and verifying — is the same pattern this paper has reported in laboratories and security work all autumn. The honest summary fits in one line: a measured 3.5 times on retired encryption, two larger estimates awaiting anyone who cares to run them.

item.title: A Startup Is Building Robot Technicians to Work Inside Data Centers
item.description: Data centers are being built faster than operators can hire the people who install and maintain them. Darwin Robotics, founded by two brothers in San Francisco, has raised $3.6 million to build robots that learn technician work by watching people do it, with first deployments aimed at early 2027.

item.title: Crushed Shells Mixed Into Beach Sand Helped Young Clams Grow in More Acidic Water
item.description: Adding shell fragments to the sand where baby clams burrow changed the water between the grains, lowered its acidity, and produced larger shells — a measured version of a shell-adding practice Indigenous communities have used for generations.

item.title: Pines Planted Far From Home Grow Up to Four Times Faster, and Handle Drought Better
item.description: Across 192 sites on four continents, conifers planted in the Southern Hemisphere outgrew the same species at home — and stored more sugars and starches, a reserve that appears to carry them through dry spells.

item.title: Claude Can Now Read Your Bank Account — Read-Only, Through Plaid, for Paid Subscribers in the United States
item.description: Anthropic announced Personal Finance in Claude on November 5: a beta for Pro, Max and Ultra subscribers in the United States that links bank, card, loan and investment accounts through Plaid and answers questions about the user’s own money in plain language. Access is read-only — Claude cannot move, manage or invest money. Users can link up to 16 banks; Claude reads balances, credit limits and up to 24 months of transactions for shared accounts. Chats in the Personal Finance hub are not used for training, Anthropic says.
item.content:encoded:
The newest thing an AI assistant can do with your money is look at it. Anthropic’s Personal Finance, rolling out in beta since November 5 to US subscribers on its paid individual plans, connects through Plaid — the service most finance apps use to reach your bank, where you sign in on Plaid’s screen, so your password never reaches Claude. You choose the accounts. For each one Claude can read the balance, the credit limit and up to two years of transactions, and answer questions in ordinary language: where the money went, what a subscription costs over a year, what changed since summer. It cannot pay, transfer, cancel or invest. The read-only line is the product.

The details carry the trade-offs. The feature exists on personal plans only — not Free, not Team, not Enterprise — and moving a personal account into a Team workspace unlinks the banks. It cannot be used inside scheduled tasks or Claude Code, so the assistant that sees your accounts cannot act on them elsewhere. OpenAI launched a similar Plaid-based feature in May, first on its $200-a-month Pro plan; Anthropic’s starts at its standard paid tiers. Whether people hand a chatbot their bank history is now a live experiment running in both companies at once. The price of finding out is one toggle, and the companies have arranged it so the finding-out cannot cost the user a transfer.

item.title: Cells Can Now Record What They Were Doing Days Ago
item.description: Engineered organelles archive a cell’s own RNA as it works — so days later, researchers can read back which genes were active, including in the rare cancer cells that survive chemotherapy and seed relapse.

item.title: A Structure Called the Cat’s Tail Records a Pluto-Scale Collision 63 Light-Years Away
item.description: Hubble has imaged the Cat’s Tail in visible light for the first time: a dark stream about 1,000 times the Earth–Sun distance across, inside a young star’s debris disk — evidence of a collision between bodies the size of Pluto.

item.title: An Arctic Ocean Bacterium Appears to Live on Acetone and Carbon Dioxide
item.description: In the cold, food-scarce water of the Arctic Ocean, a bacterium appears to build what it needs to grow out of two unlikely ingredients: acetone, the chemical in nail-polish remover, and carbon dioxide dissolved in seawater.

item.title: Starving Ants Protect Their Brains’ Energy First, Like Humans Do
item.description: When food runs short, ants keep supplying their brains at a rate comparable to the share humans protect — even though a colony is supposed to put the group ahead of any individual.

item.title: Anthropic Paid a News Publisher for the First Time, Adweek Reports: a License for AP Election Data
item.description: Adweek reported on November 4, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Anthropic struck a content and data licensing deal with the Associated Press just before the November 3 midterms — its first paid license with a digital news publisher. Claude users asking about the election saw up-to-date information provided by, and credited to, the AP. Neither company has confirmed the deal on the record; the financial terms and duration were not disclosed. In August, Anthropic told publishers it had no licensing plans, citing fair use.
item.content:encoded:
For two years the licensing question in AI had a fixed map: OpenAI signed publishers — more than a dozen deals — and Anthropic declined, telling digital publishers in August that it had no licensing plans and resting on fair use. Adweek’s report, carried in ExchangeWire’s November 9 digest, redraws one corner of that map. On election night, Claude users asking for polling information received up-to-date answers credited to the Associated Press, under what Adweek calls Anthropic’s first content and data license with a digital publisher, struck just before the midterms on the account of two people familiar with the matter.

The sourcing standard matters here, and this item carries it on its face: neither Anthropic nor the AP has confirmed the deal on the record, no announcement has been found on either company’s channels, and the price, length and scope — election data only, or something wider — are all undisclosed. The AP is the natural first counterparty: it was also the first publisher to license to Google and to OpenAI, and most of its revenue already comes from licensing. What one narrow election-window license would mean is limited; what it would start is not. Anthropic is simultaneously defending copyright suits, including the music-publishing cases in this paper’s dossiers, and preparing to sell shares to public investors who will ask how its content arrives. A first paid license, if confirmed, is the cheapest possible answer to that question — and the first step of every licensing program starts exactly this way.

item.title: A 237-Million-Year-Old Amphibian Appears to Have Lived Its Whole Life in the Ocean
item.description: No amphibian lives in the sea today. Chemical signatures in two armored fossils found in China match seawater, not the local rock — evidence of a marine amphibian 30 kilometers from the nearest possible island.

item.title: A Ring With a Screen, a Joystick and a Microphone Wants to Run Your AI Agents
item.description: Aina’s titanium ring puts a tiny screen, a thumb joystick, a microphone and a speaker on your finger, so you can approve what an AI agent does next, dictate notes and take calls without reaching for your phone. Preorders opened Thursday at $399.

item.title: Every Frontier AI Agent Tested Could Be Conned by a Fake Spouse or a Fake Screenshot
item.description: A new test, built from real fraud cases, has fake partners and colleagues talk AI agents into sending money or handing over data — the way con artists work on people. All seven frontier models tested fell for it some of the time: between 7 and 35 of every 100 attempts succeeded.
